content: 1. McKibbon KA, Wilczynski NL, and Haynes RB developed optimal search strategies for retrieving qualitative studies in PsycINFO, as published in Eval Health Prof in 2006. Their work provides a systematic approach to improving the identification of qualitative research in this database. 2. Bermúdez-Tamayo C et al. explored barriers and enablers in implementing a program aimed at reducing cesarean deliveries. Their findings, published in Reprod Health in 2017, highlight the multifaceted challenges and facilitators in achieving this goal. 3. Chaillet N et al. identified barriers and facilitators to implementing guidelines for reducing cesarean section rates in Quebec. Their study, published in the Bull World Health Organ in 2007, provides insights into the practical application of evidence-based guidelines. 4. Melman S et al. examined the perspectives of healthcare professionals on barriers and facilitators for optimal cesarean section care. Their findings, published in BMC Pregnancy Childbirth in 2017, emphasize the importance of professional input in improving cesarean care practices. 5. Pantoja T et al. conducted an overview of systematic reviews on implementation strategies for health systems in low-income countries. Their work, published in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2017, provides a comprehensive analysis of strategies to enhance healthcare delivery in resource-limited settings. 6. Ciapponi A et al. reviewed delivery arrangements for health systems in low-income countries, as published in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2017. Their findings offer evidence-based recommendations for improving maternal and neonatal care. 7. Wiysonge CS et al. analyzed financial arrangements for health systems in low-income countries, as detailed in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2017. Their study evaluates the impact of financial incentives and policies on healthcare outcomes. 8. The Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) group proposed risk of bias criteria for EPOC reviews in 2017. These criteria aim to standardize the assessment of bias in systematic reviews of healthcare interventions. 9. Sterne JAC et al. introduced the ROBINS-I tool for assessing the risk of bias in non-randomized studies of interventions. Published in BMJ in 2016, this tool provides a robust framework for evaluating methodological quality. 10. Walsh D and Downe S appraised the quality of qualitative research in midwifery, as published in Midwifery in 2006. Their work emphasizes the importance of rigorous evaluation in qualitative studies. 11. Lincoln YS and Guba EG's seminal book Naturalistic Inquiry, published in 1985, remains a foundational text for qualitative research methodology. 12. Noblit GW and Hare RD's Meta-Ethnography: Synthesizing Qualitative Studies, published in 1988, provides a methodological framework for synthesizing qualitative research findings. 13. Sandall J et al. compared midwife-led continuity models with other models of care for childbearing women in a systematic review published in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2016. Their findings support the benefits of midwife-led care in improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. 14. Bohren MA et al. reviewed the effects of continuous support for women during childbirth, as published in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2017. Their analysis highlights the positive impact of continuous support on birth outcomes. 15. Walker DM et al. evaluated the impact of the PRONTO program, a simulation-based training initiative for obstetric and neonatal emergencies, in Mexico. Their findings, published in Simul Healthc in 2016, demonstrate the program's effectiveness in improving team performance and outcomes. 16. The International Weight Management in Pregnancy (i-WIP) Collaborative Group conducted a meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomized trials to assess the effects of diet and physical activity interventions on gestational weight gain and pregnancy outcomes. Their findings, published in BMJ in 2017, provide evidence for the benefits of lifestyle interventions during pregnancy. 17. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition) provides comprehensive guidance on developing and implementing health guidelines. This resource, accessed in 2018, is a critical tool for evidence-based practice. 18. Brouwers MC et al. advanced guideline development, reporting, and evaluation in healthcare through the AGREE II instrument, as published in CMAJ in 2010. This tool standardizes the appraisal of clinical practice guidelines. 19. Bergström M et al. compared the effects of natural childbirth preparation with standard antenatal education on epidural rates, childbirth experiences, and parental stress in a randomized controlled trial published in BJOG in 2009. Their findings highlight the benefits of tailored childbirth preparation. 20. Valiani M et al. assessed the impact of childbirth training workshops on knowledge, attitudes, and delivery methods among mothers and couples in Iran. Their study, published in Iran J Nurs Midwifery Res in 2014, underscores the importance of education in promoting informed decision-making. 21. Masoumi SZ et al. evaluated the effect of childbirth preparation training on fear of vaginal delivery and delivery method choice among pregnant women in Iran. Their randomized controlled trial, published in J Family Reprod Health in 2016, demonstrates the effectiveness of educational interventions in reducing fear and promoting vaginal delivery. 22. Feinberg ME et al. examined the effects of a psychosocial couple-based prevention program on adverse birth outcomes, as published in Matern Child Health J in 2015. Their findings highlight the role of psychosocial support in improving maternal and neonatal health. 23. Fenwick J et al. evaluated the impact of a midwife psycho-education intervention on reducing childbirth fear and improving birth outcomes and postpartum psychological well-being. Their study, published in BMC Pregnancy Childbirth in 2015, supports the integration of psycho-education into maternity care. 24. Wang X et al. investigated the effects of pelvic floor muscle training as a persistent nursing intervention on delivery outcomes and pelvic floor myodynamia. Their findings, published in Int J Nurs Sci in 2014, emphasize the benefits of targeted physical interventions during pregnancy. 25. Rouhe H et al. conducted a randomized trial to assess obstetric outcomes after interventions for severe fear of childbirth in nulliparous women. Their study, published in BJOG in 2013, highlights the importance of addressing psychological factors in maternity care. 26. Sharifirad G et al. surveyed the effects of educating husbands of pregnant women on knowledge, attitudes, and reducing elective cesarean sections. Their findings, published in J Educ Health Promot in 2013, underscore the role of family involvement in promoting vaginal delivery. 27. Bastani F et al. evaluated the impact of relaxation education on adverse pregnancy outcomes in anxious primigravid Iranian women. Their randomized controlled trial, published in J Perinat Neonatal Nurs in 2006, demonstrates the benefits of relaxation techniques during pregnancy. 28. Montgomery AA et al. compared two decision aids for mode of delivery among women with previous cesarean sections in a randomized controlled trial published in BMJ in 2007. Their findings highlight the importance of decision aids in supporting informed choices. 29. Shorten A et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial of a decision aid for informed birth after cesarean, as published in Birth in 2005. Their study emphasizes the value of decision aids in promoting shared decision-making. 30. Saisto T et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial of an intervention for fear of childbirth, as published in Obstet Gynecol in 2001. Their findings highlight the effectiveness of targeted interventions in reducing childbirth fear. 31. The WHO recommendations on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections provide evidence-based strategies for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. These recommendations emphasize the importance of education, advocacy, and system-level changes. 32. Navaee M and Abedian Z evaluated the effect of role-play education on primiparous women's fear of natural delivery and their decision on the mode of delivery. Their findings, published in Iran J Nurs Midwifery Res in 2015, support the use of interactive educational methods. 33. Eden KB et al. compared two decision tools for pregnant women with prior cesareans in a randomized comparative trial published in J Obstet Gynecol Neonatal Nurs in 2014. Their study highlights the role of decision tools in facilitating informed choices. 34. Fraser W et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial of a prenatal vaginal birth after cesarean education and support program, as published in Am J Obstet Gynecol in 1997. Their findings demonstrate the benefits of targeted education and support. 35. Rouhe H et al. evaluated the life satisfaction, general well-being, and costs of treatment for severe fear of childbirth in nulliparous women through psychoeducational group or conventional care attendance. Their study, published in Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand in 2015, underscores the importance of addressing psychological well-being in maternity care. 36. Contreras A et al. developed the SOL formulas for converting SMOG readability scores between health education materials written in Spanish, English, and French. Their work, published in J Health Commun in 1999, provides a tool for improving the accessibility of health education materials. 37. Finlayson K and Downe S conducted a meta-synthesis of qualitative studies to explore why women in lowand middle-income countries do not use antenatal services. Their findings, published in PLoS Med in 2013, highlight the barriers to accessing antenatal care. 38. Althabe F et al. conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate the impact of mandatory second opinions on reducing unnecessary cesarean sections in Latin America. Their findings, published in Lancet in 2004, support the use of second opinions in clinical decision-making. 39. Liang WH et al. assessed the effect of peer review and trial of labor on lowering cesarean section rates, as published in J Chin Med Assoc in 2004. Their study highlights the role of peer review in improving clinical practices. 40. Osis MJ et al. explored Brazilian doctors' perspectives on the second opinion strategy before a cesarean section, as published in Rev Saude Publica in 2006. Their findings provide insights into the acceptance and challenges of implementing second opinion policies. 41. Chaillet N et al. conducted a cluster-randomized trial to reduce cesarean delivery rates in Quebec, as published in N Engl J Med in 2015. Their study demonstrates the effectiveness of evidence-based interventions in reducing cesarean rates. 42. Lomas J et al. compared the effectiveness of opinion leaders versus audit and feedback in implementing practice guidelines for delivery after previous cesarean sections. Their findings, published in JAMA in 1991, highlight the role of leadership in promoting guideline adherence. 43. Scarella A et al. evaluated the impact of medical audit using the Ten Group Classification System on cesarean section rates, as published in Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol in 2011. Their study underscores the importance of systematic audits in improving clinical outcomes. 44. Mohammadi S et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of clinical audits as a strategy for reducing cesarean section rates in a general hospital in Tehran, Iran. Their findings, published in J Reprod Med in 2012, highlight the practical application of audits in maternity care. 45. Poma PA evaluated the effect of departmental policies on cesarean delivery rates in a community hospital, as published in Obstet Gynecol in 1998. Their study emphasizes the role of institutional policies in influencing clinical practices. 46. Johri M et al. conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of a cluster-randomized trial to reduce cesarean delivery rates in Quebec, as published in BMC Med in 2017. Their findings provide economic evidence for implementing cesarean reduction strategies. 47. Rosenstein MG et al. examined the association of expanded access to a collaborative midwifery and laborist model with cesarean delivery rates, as published in Obstet Gynecol in 2015. Their study highlights the benefits of collaborative care models in reducing cesarean rates. 48. Keeler EB and Fok T analyzed the impact of equalizing physician fees on cesarean rates, as published in Med Care Res Rev in 1996. Their findings suggest that financial incentives alone may not significantly influence cesarean rates. 49. Lo JC evaluated the effect of financial incentives on cesarean section rates in Taiwan, as published in Health Policy in 2008. Their study highlights the limitations of financial incentives in changing clinical practices. 50. The WHO standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities provide a comprehensive framework for enhancing care delivery. These standards, accessed in 2018, emphasize evidence-based practices and patient-centered care. 51. Duffy J et al. conducted a systematic review of core outcome sets in women's and newborn health, as published in BJOG in 2017. Their findings highlight the importance of standardized outcomes in improving research and clinical care. 52. Hoffmann TC et al. developed the TIDieR checklist and guide for better reporting of interventions, as published in BMJ in 2014. This tool aims to improve the transparency and reproducibility of intervention studies. 53. The Executive Guideline Steering Group for Updating WHO Maternal and Perinatal Health Recommendations (2017–2019) provides updated evidence-based recommendations for improving maternal and perinatal health. These guidelines emphasize the importance of continuous updates to reflect the latest evidence.
